title: The farewell admonition
hookLine: an admonition that made eyes weep: hold to my sunnah and the rightly guided after me (Nawawi 28, al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah)
tomorrow: Mu'adh asks what leads to the Garden. why does it end at his tongue?
last: THE BASICS, DONE WELL · PURITY IS HALF · NO OPPRESSION

cards: A talk so moving the listeners cried: what did they ask for next? Graduation speeches, last days at a job, goodbyes at an airport gate. The jokes fade; the one line near the end tends to stay.
Last words are the ones people tend to keep. Al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah says the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, once gave them an admonition that made hearts tremble and eyes weep.
Someone said: this sounds like a farewell. So advise us.

teach.b: That's al-Nawawi's twenty-eighth hadith, from Sunan Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, in paraphrase. He counseled them to be mindful of Allah, and to listen and obey, even if the one put in charge is a slave.
Whoever lives on among you will see a great deal of disagreement.
So hold to my sunnah and the sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs after me; bite onto it with your molars. And beware of newly invented matters.

teach.h: BITE ON IT WITH YOUR MOLARS.
teach.b: Molars. Not the front teeth, the ones that nibble. The back ones, the ones that grip and don't let go, even while the rest of the mouth is busy talking.
It's a picture of holding on while something pulls the other way.
When everyone's arguing, keep your grip. A grip isn't a fist swinging at everyone else. It's teeth closed on what you were given, while the noise goes past.

It echoes an earlier day of this block, too: keep it as it came. Beware of newly invented matters is the same worry, that what's handed down gets quietly rewritten. And it's a good place to stand at the end of two weeks.
The basics. The water. The tip jar.
The beads. The joints. The heart.
Not a list to master all at once. One or two things to bite down on.

how: Muslims cite this hadith on keeping to the sunnah through disagreement; Sunni teachers name the rightly guided caliphs as Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali, and the 'molars' image is often quoted on its own.

o: the Prophet's last sermon, given during the Hajj
a warning never to ask questions about faith
a parting charge: hold fast to the Prophet's way

games.q: the farewell admonition — tap the pairs.
p: the grip that doesn't let go
what whoever lives on will see

s: the molars are a picture of a loose, easy hold
they're the back teeth, the ones that grip.
the listeners asked for advice because it sounded like a farewell
this sounds like a farewell, so advise us.

games.q: you're leaving for college next year. your dad asks what from home you'll actually keep. by today's hadith?
o: pick one or two practices and grip them through the disagreements.
hold everything loosely so nobody thinks you're too religious.
decide later; you'll know what to keep once you're there.
games.why: the charge was a grip, not a shrug: hold to the sunnah, bite on it with your molars, when disagreement comes.

practice: Write by hand one practice you want to keep a grip on: a sunnah of the Prophet's, like a greeting or a smile, or one thing from these two weeks. One line, no explaining.
Then hold the paper for the sit, grip light but steady, the way you'd hold something you plan to keep.

wordCard.voice: The farewell admonition: the talk that made eyes weep, and its charge: hold to the sunnah, and hold it with your molars.

orig.note: Arabic: the molars, the back teeth; 'bite onto it with the molars.'

carryVoice: To keep: hold it with your molars, the back teeth, the ones that don't let go. Two weeks of the forty, carried.

sources.ref: al-Nawawi, al-Arba'in, hadith 28; Sunan Abu Dawud 4607, Jami' al-Tirmidhi 2676 (al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah)
